uploads/science/Microscope Coloring.pdf.searchText: Microscope Coloring http://www.biologycorner.com/worksheets/microscope_coloring.html Name: ___________________________________________ Color the Microscope Parts The most familiar type of microscope is the standard light microscope. The base (L) and arm (G) are usually one single piece of cast metal. The arm is the correct place to grip the microscope when carrying it while supporting the base with the palm of your other hand. Color the arm green and the base red. The stage (I) is the platform that supports the specimen to be observed. The stage has a hole in its center to allow light to pass through, so specimens must be positioned over the top of this hole. Color the stage blue. You can control how much light goes through the specimen by adjusting the diaphragm (K). It has a range of 1 to 5, with 5 being the most light. Color the diaphragm light green. Since any slight movement of the specimen is magnified many times, the slide is usually held down by a pair of stage clips (J). Color the stage clips gray. Light microscopes use either a bulb or a mirror (M) as their light source. Never use direct sunlight; it may damage your eyes. Color the light source yellow. The switch for this light is usually found on the base of the microscope, and sometimes on the power cord. After the light has passed through the specimen, it enters the objective lens (often called "objective" for short). The shortest of the three objectives is the scanning-power objective lens (N), and has a power of 4X. Color the 4X objective black. The second objective is the low-power objective (F), which is almost always made to produce a magnification of 10 times (10X). Color the low-power objective purple. The high-power objective lens (H) has a magnification of 40X. Draw orange stripes on the high-power objective. The body tube (C) allows the light from the objective to pass upward to form the first magnified image; that image is further magnified by the eyepiece or ocular (A). The eyepiece is usually 10X. Color the body tube brown and the ocular lens orange. The total magnification obtained is the product of the eyepiece times that of the objective lens. You can easily switch objectives by turning the rotating nosepiece (E). Color the nosepiece blue-green. The coarse adjustment knob (B) is the larger on your microscope. You will use this primarily to focus on your specimen. DO NOT USE THE COARSE ADJUSTMENT KNOB ON HIGH POWER (40X), it will crack your slide. Color this knob pink. The fine adjustment knob (D) is also for minute focusing. You use this after you have focused with the coarse adjustment knob. Color this knob tan. The top part of the microscope that supports the ocular lens and the objective lens is not labeled on your image. Color this area to match the base. QUESTIONS: 1. What two structures on the microscope will you use to focus on your specimen? __________________________________________ 2. Why should you never use the coarse adjustment knob on high power? ___________________________________________________________________________________________ 3. What will happen if you use direct sunlight to observe your specimen? ______________________________________________________________________________________ 4. Our microscopes have three objectives. What are their powers?________________________ 5. What is the magnification of the ocular lens? ____________________ 6. What is the shortest objective called? ________________________________________ 7. How do you switch objectives?____________________________________________________________ 8. Which structure controls how much light passes through the specimen?______________________ 9. You should carry the microscope by placing your palm on the _____________________ and gripping the ___________________ with your other hand. 10. How can you prevent your slide from slipping on the stage?________________________________ 1 of 2 8/29/2014 9:19 AM Microscope Coloring http://www.biologycorner.com/worksheets/microscope_coloring.html 2 of 2 8/29/2014 9:19 AM

Credit is given for the original activity to Mr. Buckley. Original can be accessed at: https://www.rcsdk12.org/cms/lib04/NY01001156/Centricity/Domain/4824/Introductiontothe MicroscopeLab.pdf Objectives: 1. Demonstrate the proper procedures used in correctly using the compound light microscope. 2. Determine the total magnification of the microscope. 3. Explain how to properly handle the microscope. 4. Describe the changes in the field of view and available light when going from low to high power using the compound light microscope 5. Explain how to increase the amount of light when going from low to high power using the compound light microscope. 6. Explain the proper procedure for focusing under low and high power using the compound light microscope. Materials: • Compound microscope • Materials to create a slide from a letter from newsprint: o blank glass slides o cover slips o eye dropper o beaker of water o letter "e" cut from newsprint (or any letter your choose) o scissors Procedures: Part 1. Microscope handling 1. Carry the microscope with both hands --- one on the arm and the other under the base of the microscope. 2. One person from each group will now go over to the microscope storage area and properly transport one microscope to your working area. 3. The other person in the group will pick up a pair of scissors, newsprint, a slide, and a cover slip, if preparing your own slide. Examine the microscope and put the number of the part for the function of each of the parts listed on the right side of the diagram. body tube stage clip low power objective mirror (many microscopes have a light instead) base eyepiece or ocular coarse adjustment arm diaphragm inclination joint nosepiece fine adjustment knob Indicate the parts of the microscope (correct number) and their functions. You may use a separate sheet for the answers. Development and distribution funded by the National Science Foundation Part 2. Determining total magnification: Locate the numbers on the eyepiece and the low power objective and fill in the blanks below. Eyepiece magnification Objective magnification Total Magnification (X) = X Do the same for the high power objective. Eyepiece magnification Objective magnification Total Magnification (X) = X Write out the rule for determining total magnification of a compound microscope. Part 3. Preparing and viewing a wet mount of the letter "e” or any letter of your choosing. Preparation: 1. With your scissors, cut out the letter "e" from the newspaper. 2. Place it on the glass slide as it would look like when reading. 3. Cover the letter with a clean cover slip. See the figure below. Note: the “e” will be much smaller than in the example below. 4. Using your eyedropper, place a drop of water on the edge of the cover slip where it touches the glass slide. The water should be sucked under the slide if done properly. Viewing: 1. Turn on the microscope and place the slide on the stage; making sure the "e" is facing the normal reading position (see the figure above). Using the coarse focus and low power, move the body tube down until the "e" can be seen clearly. Draw what you see in the space below. All drawings should be neat and drawn with pencils. Development and distribution funded by the National Science Foundation Total magnification: 2. Describe the relationship between what you see through the eyepiece and what you see on the stage. 3. Offer an explanation of why this happened. 4. Looking through the eyepiece, move the slide to the upper right area of the stage. What direction does the image move? 5. Now, move it to the lower left side of the stage. What direction does the image move? 6. Re-center the slide and change the scope to high power. You will notice the "e" is out of focus. Do Not touch the coarse focus knob, instead use the fine focus to resolve the picture. Draw the image you see of the letter e (or part of it) on high power. Concluding Questions: 1. Discuss 3 procedures which should be used to properly handle a light microscope. 2. Explain why the light microscope is also called the compound microscope. 3. Images observed under the light microscope are reversed and inverted. Explain what this means. 4. Explain why the specimen must be centered in the field of view on low power before going to high power. 5. A microscope has a 20 X ocular (eyepiece) and two objectives of 10 X and 43 X respectively: 6. Calculate the low power magnification of this microscope. Show your formula and all work. uploads/science/microscope_worksheet.pdf.searchText: Oct. 00 a.Lee Name:_______________________________ Date:___________________ Period: _______ Microscope Worksheet I. How Can a Microscope Help Us Study Living Things? Microscope: an instrument that makes things look bigger Biology: the study of living things. Some living things are so small we can’t see them with the naked eye alone. Many of these are one celled organisms called PROTOZOA [pro tuh ZO uh] and BACTERIA. We can see such tiny things with the help of a high-power microscope. A microscope magnifies, or makes things look bigger. Have you ever used a magnifying glass? It is a simple microscope. A magnifying glass, or hand lens, is easy to use. It doesn’t weigh much, and it’s easy to carry. But it doesn’t magnify objects very much. We still cannot see one-celled plants and animals with a hand lens. A compound microscope is much more powerful than a simple microscope. Most school microscopes are compound microscope. They can make objects look 100 to 400 times as big as they really are. Some compound microscopes magnify more than a thousand times. When we say “microscope,” we usually mean a compound microscope. The microscope has many uses, especially in biology – the study of living things. Doctors often use microscopes. Is there one in your doctor’s office? Parts of the Microscope Eyepiece: Lens closes to the eye. High Power Objective: Longer of the two lenses close to the slide. Lower Power Objective: Shorter of the two lenses close to the slide. Tube: Gives the distance needed between the eyepiece and objective. Coarse Adjustment Knob: Moves the tube up and down. Fine Adjustment Knob: Also moves the tube up and down but only slightly. Base: Holds up the entire microscope. Arm: Holds the tube and lenses. Connects to the base. Nosepiece: Holds objective lenses. Light: Shines light into the tube. Diaphragm: Circular disk that lets more or less light pass through. Stage: Platform for slide to rest. An opening in its center lets light pass through. Clips(2): Hold the slide in place on the stage. II. How Does a Microscope Magnify? There are three lenses in the microscope. The Eyepiece Objective Lens Magnification top lens is called the eyepiece. It is the lens closest to 10x 10x 100x the eye. The other two lenses are called objectives. 10x 40x These are the lenses closest to the object. The object is 10x 44x on a microscope slide. Different lenses magnify in 5x 10x different powers. The power of magnification is marked 5x 40x by a number with an x next to it. A lens that magnifies 20x 10x ten times is marked 10x. If the eyepiece is marked 10x and the objective 10x, then the total magnification is 100x. To find the total magnification of a microscope, just multiply the two magnifications. Complete the table below by finding the total magnification for each pair of lenses. III. Handling Microscope. A microscope is a delicate instrument. Treat it carefully. 1. Matching. Match the two lists. Write the correct letter on the line next to each number. 1. ______ simple microscope a) support entire microscope. 2. ______ base b) has one lens only. 3. ______ compound microscope c) study of living things. 4. ______ eyepiece d) has more than one lens. 5. ______ biology e) lens closest to the eye. VII. True or false. Write T on the line next to the number if the sentence is true. Write F if the sentence is false. 1. ______ A microscope makes things bigger. (Careful, this is tricky!) 2. ______ A microscope can have one lens. 3. ______ Compound microscopes are used on nature walks. 4. ______ A compound microscope magnifies more than a simple microscope does. 5. ______ Light enters the eyepiece first. 6. ______ A microscope stage must have an opening. 7. ______ When you carry a microscope, you should hold it by the tube. 8. ______ Focusing upward can crack a slide. 9. ______ You should use only lens tissue to clean a microscope lens. uploads/science/Microscopes and cells 3..searchText: M Activity Looking at cheek cells A2 Core ? Aim To make drawings of cheek cells using the microscope. After use put the cotton bud and slide in disinfectant. Equipment l microscope l cotton buds T l microscope slides l cover slips l methylene blue l disinfectant l mounted needle What to do 1 Wipe a clean fresh cotton bud around the inside surface of your cheek and the outer lower side of the gum. 2 Dab the cotton bud on the centre of a microscope slide, add one drop of methylene blue and cover with a cover slip. The picture shows you how to do this properly. 3 Put the slide on the microscope stage and focus the microscope on a group of cells under low power. 4 Rotate the objective lens to medium power and re-focus using the fine focusing knob. 5 After use, ensure you put the cotton bud and the microscope slide directly into the disinfectant. Results Draw what you can see on a blank piece of paper. Look at Topic A2 for hints on how to do really good drawings. Make sure you give your drawing a heading and calculate the total magnification: total magnification  objective lens magnification  eyepiece lens magnification 95 q I Bradley, C Tear, M Winterbottom, S Young, 2001, The Heinemann Science Scheme M Activity Looking at other types of cell A2 Extension ? Aim To look at different types of cell under the microscope. Wear eye protection. Equipment If you get iodine solution in your eye, tell a teacher l microscope l onion immediately. l mounted needle l red petals T l microscope slides l plant roots l cover slips l potatoes l iodine solution l tomatoes l scalpel l ruler What to do 1 Peel away the dead, dry layers from the outside of an onion. Break a layer off, and peel off the thin skin (epidermis) on its inside surface. 2 If you find this difficult, crack the layer down the middle, and the skin may peel off between the two halves. 3 Cut or tear your piece of epidermis so it is no bigger than 7 mm square. Always cut with the scalpel facing away from you, and use a mat or a cutting tile. 4 Place it in the centre of a microscope slide, making sure it is flat and not folded. 5 Add one drop of iodine and cover with a cover slip. 6 Put the slide on the microscope stage and focus the microscope on a group of cells under low power. 7 Rotate the objective lens to medium power and re-focus using the fine focusing knob. Results Draw and label a group of five cells under medium power. Extension 1 You have seen how to make slides of scraped cells (cheek cells) and layers of cells (onion cells). Make new slides of petal cells, root cells, potato cells and tomato cells. Draw what you see under medium power. 2 By putting a ruler under the objective lens, measure the width of the field of view. By estimating how far across the field of view each specimen stretches, estimate the size of each specimen you have prepared. 96 q I Bradley, C Tear, M Winterbottom, S Young, 2001, The Heinemann Science Scheme M Activity How to use the microscope A2 Help ? Aim To learn how to use the microscope. Be careful with sand. It can Equipment cause serious damage if it gets into your eyes. l microscope l microscope slides l cover slips l sand T l mounted needle l newsprint What to do Preparing a slide 1 Cut out a letter ‘‘e’’ from the newspaper you have been given. 2 Place it in the centre of a microscope slide. 3 Put one drop of water on top of the letter. 4 Lower a cover slip onto the drop. The picture shows you how to do this properly. Looking at a slide 1 Put the slide on the stage, and move it under the stage clips. 2 Check that the ‘‘e’’ is above the centre of the hole in the stage. 3 Rotate the objective lenses until the shortest lens is pointing downwards as shown on the right. 4 Twist the focusing knob until the stage and objective lens are as close as they can be. 5 Look down the microscope and twist the focusing knob towards you. 6 Stop when you can see the ‘‘e’’ clearly and sharply. Increasing the magnification 1 Twist the objective lenses until the middle lens is pointing downwards. 2 Look down the microscope and twist the fine focusing knob until you can see part of the ‘‘e’’ clearly and sharply. Results 1 Draw what you see under the microscope on low power and medium power. 2 Use the same method to look at sand and hair under the microscope. 97 q I Bradley, C Tear, M Winterbottom, S Young, 2001, The Heinemann Science Scheme M Activity Making models of animal and A3 plant cells Core ? Aim To make models of an animal cell and a plant cell. Wear eye protection. Equipment If you get any of the cellulose paste in your eyes, tell a teacher immediately. l cellulose paste l two large clear plastic bags l black marker pen l one small clear plastic bag T l green marker pen l cotton or wire to be used for sealing bags l two ping-pong balls l clear plastic box l polystyrene What to do Animal cell 1 Colour a ping-pong ball black and put it into the large plastic bag. 2 Make up the cellulose paste, pour it into the bag, and seal it. Plant cell 1 Fill the small plastic bag with water, seal it, and put it into the large plastic bag. 2 Roll ten pieces of the polystyrene into small balls (smaller than the ping-pong ball) and colour them green. 3 Colour the ping-pong ball black. 4 Put the polystyrene and the ping-pong ball into the large plastic bag. 5 Make up the cellulose paste, pour it into the bag, and seal it. 6 Place the bag in the plastic box and close the lid. Question Each part of the model represents a particular part of the cell. Copy and complete the table using the words below to show how they match up. cytoplasm chloroplasts nucleus cell membrane cell wall vacuole Part of the model Part of the cell polystyrene balls plastic box small bag of water cellulose paste large plastic bag ping-pong ball 98 q I Bradley, C Tear, M Winterbottom, S Young, 2001, The Heinemann Science Scheme M Activity What do pollen grains look like? A6 Core ? Aim To examine the surface of pollen grains. Make sure you wash your Equipment hands after handling any living material. l microscope l teat pipette l microscope slide l scissors T l cover slips l paint brush l mounted needle l flower with anthers bearing pollen What to do 1 Remove one anther from your flower using the scissors. 2 Place it on your microscope slide and put it onto the microscope stage. 3 Look at the anthers under low power. Try to find the tiny round pollen grains clinging to their surface. Avoid contact with pollen, especially if you already suffer from hay fever. 4 Remove the slide from the microscope and tap the anthers onto the slide. Some pollen should drop onto the slide. If not, try using the paint brush to transfer the pollen from the anther to the slide. 5 Add one drop of water and cover with a cover slip. 6 Replace the slide on the microscope, and focus on the pollen grains under low power. 7 Twist the objective lens to medium power and focus again. Results Draw the pollen grains that you can see. You may need to look on high power to see what the pollen grains look like on their surface. 99 q I Bradley, C Tear, M Winterbottom, S Young, 2001, The Heinemann Science Scheme M Activity How does sugar concentration A6 affect pollen tube growth? Extension ? Aim To find out whether sugar concentration affects how many pollen tubes germinate. Wear eye protection. If you get any sucrose solution in your eyes, tell a teacher immediately. Avoid Equipment contact with pollen microscope scissors T l l l cavity microscope slides l paint brush l cover slips l flower with anthers bearing pollen l mounted needle l sucrose solutions (10%, 8%, 6%, 4%, l teat pipette 2%, 0%) Plan and predict 1 Write a plan for the investigation using some or all of the equipment above. When you think about your method, you need to consider: l The other variables you need to control (e.g. temperature) l How many pollen grains you need to look at to give you a reliable result l How you are going to record your results 2 Predict what you think the result will be. Before you begin any practical work, your plan must be checked by a teacher. Analyse 1 Plot a graph of your results with concentration along the x-axis (the one which goes across) and number of germinated pollen grains on the y-axis (the one which goes up). Draw a line through the points. 2 As sugar concentration increases, does the number of germinating pollen grains increase? Evaluate Compare your graph to those obtained by other groups. Are your graphs identical? If they are not, try to explain why. Answering the following questions will help get you started. l Are all pollen grains identical? l Were all anthers from the same flower? l Was it easy to see if pollen grains had germinated? l Did any results seem out of place? 100 q I Bradley, C Tear, M Winterbottom, S Young, 2001, The Heinemann Science Scheme

uploads/science/Microscopes.docx.searchText: Microscopes Use page 152 of Jacaranda Science 1 to help you compete the following activities. Using Microscopes Microscopes can be easily damaged and are very expensive. To stop accidents happening, we need to know how to handle and use them correctly. Using your book, list the six important rules to remember when using microscopes. Parts of a Microscope and their Functions Use your book to label the microscope below. What are the steps for the correct use of a microscope? Match the microscope part to its function . Eyepiece Lens The platform on which the microscope is built. Focus knob The lens you look through to see the object you are studying. Stage Positioned beneath the stage to direct light through the object you are studying. Mirror The adjustable tube between the eyepiece and the objective lens. Base Rotates to change the objective lenses. Stage Clip The platform on which the object you are studying is placed. Microscope Tube A knob that can be turned to bring the object you are studying into focus. Objective Lens The lens closest to the object you are studying. There may be more than one of these lenses. Revolving Nosepiece Holds the slide in place on the stage.

uploads/science/Microsoft_Word_-_Monohyb.searchText: Print out the following set of Monohybrid and Dihybrid problems. Complete the punnett squares and answer the question in each problem. Question Set A. Albinism is a condition in humans in which they are unable to produce the pigment melanin. People with this condition take on the color of the blood flowing through their capillaries. This occurs when the dominant normal allele (N) is absent and an individual gets two defective recessive genes (nn). 1) What phenotype would an individual with the genotype NN be? 2) What phenotype would an individual with genotype Nn be? 3) A man heterozygous for albinism has 4 children with an albino woman. What phenotypes and genotypes would you expect? What is the man’s genotype: What gene will be present in each of the man’s different gametes: , . What will be the woman’s genotype: What will be present in each of the woman’s gametes: , . In the punnett square below, place the two possible gametes for the woman at the top of each column and the two possible gametes for the man at the side of each row. Determine the genotypes of the offspring. Construct a Punnett square: 4) A couple that both have normal (dominant trait) skin color have an albino (recessive trait) child and 2 normal children. What are the parents’ genotypes? Mother’s Genotype: Father’s Genotype: Draw the punnett square showing all the possible genotypes for their children. 5) What are the chances of a couple both hybrid (heterozygous) for albinism having a ‘normal’ child? Construct a Punnett square: How many different possible children could be produced (how many squares)? How many children contain at least one dominant gene in their genotype? Divide the # showing the dominant trait by the total # of possible offspring, express as a percentage: Question Set B. Cystic Fibrosis is a disabling genetic disease that used to always cause death by the time a child was a teenager. Its cause is a recessive gene (g) that produces abnormal glycoproteins that interfere with salt metabolism. The sweat of the body is high in sodium chloride (table salt), but more important, the mucus secreted is abnormally thick and clogs passageways in the lungs, liver and pancreas. This leads to pneumonia, and liver function is impaired so bile production is reduced and fat digestion is not normal. Digestive enzymes from the pancreas are interfered with by fibrous growths. • Is Cystic Fibrosis a dominant or a recessive trait? • • What is the genotype of an individual with Cystic Fibrosis?_______ • • What are the chances of two parents that are heterozygous (carriers) of the disease having a normal child? Construct a Punnett square that shows the cross of the two parents described: Probability of having 1 normal (CF free) child: ________ % Question Set C. Most genes that cause abnormal conditions (such as albinism) are recessive. An exception to this is Chondrodystrophic dwarfism. It is caused by the presence of a dominant gene (C). Most people are homozygous recessive (cc) and have normal height. People that are hybrid or homozygous dominant for the gene are dwarfs with shortened arms and legs, which are usually also very bowed, but their torsos are of normal size. The dominant gene causes premature closure of the growth plates in the arm and leg long bones. 6) What are the chances of two ‘normal’ people having a Chondrodystrophic dwarf child? Construct a Punnett square: Di-Hybrid Crosses: 1. Hearing (D) is dominant to deafness (d), and having a normal metabolism (P) is dominant to having pku (p). A married couple, Barbie and Ken, have these phenotypes and genotypes: Barbie is ddPP (deaf but normal metabolism), and Ken is Ddpp (he can hear but has pku). They ask their genetic counselor, “What are our chances of having a ‘normal’ child? (can hear and has normal metabolism)? What is the genotype of ‘Barbie’? What is the genotype of ‘Ken’? What will be the possible gamete combinations What will be the possible gamete combinations for ‘Barbie’ for ‘Ken’ 1st of each gene pair 1st of each gene pair 1st & 2nd 1st & 2nd 2nd & 1st 2nd & 1st 2nd of each pair 2nd of each pair Draw a punnett square showing the possible offspring from Barbie and Ken. Place the gametes from Barbie across the top (four columns), and the gametes from Ken along the side (rows). XXXX XXXX BARBIE XXXX XXXX K E N How many of Barbie & Ken’s offspring will be: Deaf but with normal metabolism Deaf but with PKU Hearing but with normal metabolism Hearing but with PKU 2. In people nearsightedness (N) is dominant to normal vision (n), and polydactyly (having an ‘extra’ finger or toe) is dominant to 5-fingered hands. A man with normal vision and sho is heterozygous for polydactyly marries a heterozygous nearsighted woman with ‘normal’ hands. What are the couple’s chances (%) of having a child with normal vision and normal hands? Draw a punnett square showing the results of this cross. XXXX XXXX FEMALE XXXX XXXX M A L E

uploads/science/Mining.docx.searchText: Mining The economy in Western Australia relies heavily on mining. Mining is the removal of resource s from the ground . Resources are useful substances that humans dig up out of the ground. Resources can be classified as: _ _ _ An e xample of a resource is coal. Coal is formed from _____________that grew many years ago. They died and fell into s___________, where they were covered by s___________. High _____________, ___________ and a lack of ________ changed and c________ the dead plants to give coal. Coal is a useful resource as it can be burned to get energy. uploads/science/Mitosis notes.docx.searchText: Mitosis notes Mitosis is the name for the cell division that is responsible for growth, repair and replacement within living organisms, as well as during asexual reproduction. All the somatic cells in an organism are produced by mitosis. Only the sex cells or gametes are produced by the process of m ei osis . When a cell undergoes mitosis it splits in to two daughter cells which are identical to the original cell and to each other. Mitosis occurs in a series of phases or stages: Interphase This is sometimes described as the resting phase, but it is also the stage when the chromosomes are copied. At the start the chromosomes appear as threadlike coils ( chromatin ) but gradually take on a distinct rod like structure. By the end of interphase the cell has two copies of each chromosome and each chromosome and its copy pair up and form sister chromatids . Prophase Cell division starts; centrioles or poles appear and begin to move to opposite ends of the cell. Spindle fibres form between the poles. Metaphase The chromatids (pairs of chromosomes) line up in the centre of the cell and attach to the spindle fibres. Anaphase The spindle fibres contract and pull the chromatids apart, so one copy is at each end of the cell. Telophase Two new nuclei form (as two nuclear membranes are formed). The chromosomes appear threadlike again (chromatin) . Cytokinesis The cell membrane moves inwards and two new daughter cells are formed, each with its own nucleus and identical chromosomes. uploads/science/Motion and Energy notes.searchText: ﻿Use physics to describe the operation of technological devices, and to solve problems Introduction: Forces and Motion – Year 11 information in 1 easy lesson (plus year 12 work!) Speed & Velocity • The rate at which a body moves from one location to another is usually described as either speed (s) or velocity (v) Average velocity (ms-1) = Distance covered (m) Time taken (s) d v t • if it took 4 hours to travel from Dunedin to Christchurch which is 360km, what is the average speed? • Egs: • What is the speed of a car in kmh-1 if it covers 15km in 30 minutes? • Find the speed of a runner in ms-1 if she covers 1000m in 7 minutes. Converting Units kmh-1 is converted to ms-1 by…… x 1000 (m in km)  3600 (s in hr) ms-1 is converted to kmh-1 by ….. x 3600 1000 Egs: • A cricket ball is bowled at 134km per hour. • Convert 134 kmh-1 to ms-1 (37.22) • If the batsman is 18 m from the bowler when the ball is released, how long has he to prepare this stroke? (about 0.5 s) • Stephen fancied himself as a tennis player. He asked Peter to time his serves from the serve line to the netting fence (30m) • Find the speed of the serve in metres per second if the measured time was 1.2s. (25) • Convert this speed to kmh-1 Distance-Time Graphs d stop constant speed Acceleration • An object changing its speed is accelerating – positively or negatively (decelerating) Acceleration (ms-2) = final velocity – initial velocity (Δv) Time taken (s) v a t • Eg: Calculate acceleration of a trolley which changes from 2ms-1 to 5ms-1 in 2 seconds. Velocity-Time graphs v constant speed accn t Activity: Optional Year 11 Pathfinder: p38-9 no’s 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10,11 Vectors and Scalars • A scalar is a physical quantity that has size (magnitude) but no direction. Egs include distance, speed and temperature • A vector is a physical quantity that has both size and direction. Egs include displacement, velocity and force • A vector can be represented by an arrow. The length represents the magnitude and the arrow represents the direction. • Vectors can be added graphically by placing the tail of the second vector on the head of the first. The vector drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second vector is the resultant. It is identified by a double arrow. Eg Tom walks 6m in an easterly direction followed by 8m in a northerly direction. Find: a) the total distance Tom has travelled b) the shortest distance from the starting point. Solution: a) The total distance is 6+8 = 14m b) The shortest distance is calculated using a vector diagram and pythagoras’ theorem which states that for a right angled triangle, the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. So: √62 + 82 = √ 36 + 64 = √100 = 10m Let’s Get Moving- Checking Motion understanding! 1. Complete the table. What does a negative acceleration tell you? 5. Convert these measurements to the new units. Show your working. a) 1km = m b) 1675m = km c) 1h = s d) 720s = h e) 72kmh-1 = ms-1 f) 5 ms-1 = kmh-1 Forces – Checking what you know • Forces push, pull, tug, heave, squeeze, stretch, twist or press. • Forces change: the shape of an object the movement of an object the speed of an object • Some forces act by contact which needs to touch an object to produce an effect, eg pushing by hand, ocean waves crashing on rocks, tiny forces holding a soap film together eg thrust, support, friction (drag) • Some forces do not need contact, and can act at a distance. These are non contact or field forces eg magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic Direction and Strength of Forces • Forces can act upwards, downwards, sideways, or any direction at all. • Arrows are used to show direction of forces • Strength of force is shown by the thickness or length of an arrow. Measuring Forces • Meters that measure forces usually have springs in them. The bigger the force the more the spring is squashed or stretched. • Spring balance or forcemeter or newtonmeter are often used in schools. • A spring is stretched by the pulling force and squashed by the pushing force. • The amount of force has a unit called a newton (N) • Notice that 1kg = 10N. What would 2kg be? 0.5kg? 100kg? Balanced and Unbalanced Forces • The forces acting on an object determine how that object will move. If we push on some object and the object doesn’t move, then the force we exert must be balanced by another force. • An unbalanced force will produce acceleration Newton’s First Law of Motion If the forces acting on an object are balanced, then the object will either stay still or keep moving at the same speed in the same direction. Thus a force is needed to make something speed up or slow down or change direction. Eg. In a car crash, a large force acts on the car and quickly stops the car. However, the driver will keep on moving with the same speed in the same direction until a force slows him or her down. The force is hopefully provided by a seatbelt or airbag. Without either, the driver may continue moving right through the windscreen and out of the car. Newton’s Second Law of Motion If there are unbalanced forces acting upon an object, then the object will accelerate in the direction that the net force acts. The size of the acceleration depends upon the mass of the object and size of the force. This is illustrated by the relationship F=m.a In sport, acceleration can be improved by better force from muscular contraction or reducing the weight of the object to be moved. Eg for javelin, shotput etc you can improve strength and for running you can reduce weight. Laboratory: Tug of War Acceleration due to Gravity • A free falling object has an acceleration of 9.8ms-2 (more commonly rounded to 10ms-2). This means that each second its speed will increase by 10ms-2 until it reaches terminal velocity Laboratory: Determining acceleration due to gravity Tug-O-War What to do: • Have one person hold the trolley still in the middle of the bench • By varying the sizes of m1 and m2 set up each force arrangement shown in the table below • When each arrangement is ready, record F1 and F2 then let the trolley go and observe the motion. NB: Catch the trolley before it crashes or else! Results: Arrangement F1(N) F2 (N) Net force (N) Observation with respect to acceleration F1 >>>>>F2 F1 > F2 F1 = F2 F1 < F2 F1 <<<< F2 Conclusion: Write a statement which summarises your findings. Determining the Acceleration of Gravity Materials: strong thread, large metal washers, retort stand, metre ruler, stopwatch Principles and Method: • When a body accelerates, its velocity changes over time. For eg; if you drop a ball from the top of a tree, gravity pulls on the ball and causes it to move faster and faster toward the ground. If a body has an acceleration of 9.8ms­­-2, this means that after one second, the body has a velocity of 9.8ms-1‑, after 2 seconds, a velocity of 19.6ms-1 and so on. • Gravity is a force that causes the pendulum to accelerate and swing back and forth. We will use a pendulum to find the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity because the pendulum executes simple harmonic motion. T= 2Π T= the period of the pendulum, l is the length of the pendulum, and g is the acceleration of gravity. There is no mass in the formula indicating the period (time) is independent of mass. • Pull the pendulum back 10-15º and release. Measure the time required for the pendulum to swing 10 times, and divide by 10 to find the average T. Substitute this value and the measured length of the pendulum (from retort stand to washer) into the following equation and solve for g: g= • Record your results in the table below. Repeat with 3 different lengths of pendulum, and calculate an average value of g. The accepted value for the acceleration is 9.8ms­­-2. What experimental errors might you have made? • Calculate the relative error of your values of g using the following formula: Relative error= (observed – accepted) * 100% = ( your g – 9.8) * 100% = Accepted 9.8 Length of pendulum (m) TRIAL- period T (s) Average calculated acceleration of gravity g (ms-2) Average Relative error % 1 2 3 Mass and Weight • Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg. The mass of an objects is the same regardless of where it is located in the universe. • The weight of an object is the force of gravity that acts on the object. The weight of an object depends on where it is located in the universe. • Weight is measured in newtons (N) because it is a force. • Weight can be calculated from Fw = m.g where g is the acceleration due to gravity and on earth, is accepted as 10Nkg-1. • The weight of an object on the moon is 1/6 that on Earth because the gravitational field strength is less. Worksheets • Some ‘quick’ problems • ESA book (y11) • 12 physics pathfinder exercises. Equilibrium • When the resultant force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. • In this case, the object is either not moving (static equilibrium) or it is moving in a straight line at constant speed (dynamic equilibrium). Some ‘Quick’ Problems 1. The diagram shows the forces being applied to a 160kg bicycle and rider. a) what is the direction and size of the nett force acting on the bike and rider? b) Calculate the acceleration of the bike and rider. Give the correct unit with your answer. 2. A motorbike with its rider has an acceleration of 10ms-2. The nett force exerted by the engine is 5800N. Calculate the combined mass of bike and the rider. 3. How would the acceleration of a dragster be affected if the following changes were applied? a) the mass of the dragster remains constant but…… i) the engine is tuned up to give twice the force ii) the engine is de-tuned to give half the force b) the engine force remains constant but….. i) the mass of the dragster is doubled ii) the mass of the dragster is halved. Torque -Optional reading from pp167-9 for Torque. • Forces are often used to rotate or turn objects – this turning effect is called a torque or moment. • The turning of a door handle, using a spanner to tighten a nut and the force applied to the pedal of a bicycle are examples of torques. • The torque is always stated relative to a point called the pivot. • To describe a torque, the size of the force and the perpendicular distance between the line of action of the force and the pivot must be known. • Torque is calculated as: T = F. d⊥ Where F = Force and d⊥ = perpendicular distance between line of action at force and pivot • The SI unit for torque is the Newton-metre, Nm. The direction of the torque is usually stated as being clockwise or anticlockwise Balanced Ruler • A suspended ruler was balanced by moving a mass-stack to a position where the ruler no longer turns. • The weight F of the mass-stack produces a clockwise torque Tc = Fd1 where d1 is the distance of the point of suspension of the mass stack from the pivot. • The weight Fg of the ruler acts through its centre of gravity. • The weight Fg of the ruler produces an anit-clockwise torque TA = Fgd2 where d2 is the distance of the centre of gravity of the ruler from the pivot. • The balanced suspended ruler is said to be in rotational equilibrium as it obeys the principle of turning moments Principle of Turning Moments For an object in

uploads/science/Motion energy 2009 .doc.searchText: ﻿ Motion energy is correctly termed kinetic energy (you may remember this from last year). It is the energy something posesses if it has movement, for example a bullet has a lot of kinetic energy because it is moving very fast. This kind of energy is of great interest to athletes as it is how they will win their race! Stability is also an important aspect of sport, whether you are a javelin thrower, a gymnast or a sprinter you will want to maximise stability in a variety of positions. 1. CENTRE OF MASS The centre of mass of a sportsperson is the single point through which the whole mass of the body can be seen to act. The postion of the centre of mass can affect the balance of an athlete. Examples of the effect of the centre of mass include; gymnasts whose centre of mass is off centre at inappropriate times can lose their balance; divers with the same problem will have trouble executing a high scoring dive. Weightlifters stand with their feet apart to lower their centre of mass and give them greater stability (ASTA, 2000). ACTIVITY 1: Determining the Centre of Mass Materials: 1 Plumb-bob 1 sheet of shapes to cut out scissors, glue, poster paper The centre of mass can be determined using a plumb-bob, which consists of a piece of thread with a mass on one end. Method: 1. Cut out the model. 2. Push a pin into any point on the model and tie the plumb-bob to the pin. 3. Trace the vertical line on the model formed by the hanging thread. 4. Push the pin into another point on the model and again trace the vertical line formed by the hanging thread. 5. The point where these two lines intersect is the centre of mass. Mark it with a big X 6. Now cut out the remainder of the figures, find their centre of mass. 7. Place them in correct order to show the changes in the centre of mass of an athlete performing the long jump. 8. Glue to the paper provided and write an appropriate heading to explain your series of figures. 2. FORCES Forces are a very important part of our every day life. While we may not want to execute a triple cartwheel with a round off on our way to school we want to be able to get off the bus safely and manage walking up and down stairs and getting around in general. Mass is the amount of matter in an object (and has the unit of kg). Weight is a measure of the force of gravity on an object (and has the unit of N). Thus, mass of an object remains constant no matter where the object is. However, the weight of an object varies, depending on the force of gravity being exerted on the object. Weight and mass are related according to the equation weight = mass x "g" where "g" is the force of gravity. If weight has the unit of N and mass the unit of kg then "g" will have the unit of N/kg (Newtons per kilogram). On earth "g" has the value of approximately 9.8 Nkg. Distance-Time Graphs Plotting distance against time can tell you a lot about motion. Let’s look at the axes: Time is always plotted along the bottom on the X-axis . The further to the right on the axis, the longer the time from the start. Distance is plotted up the left had side of the graph on the Y-axis . The higher up the graph, the further the distance from the starting point. 438150 142875 If an object is not moving, a horizontal line is shown on a distance-time graph. 504825 116840 Time is increasing to the right but the distance does not change. The object is not moving so we say it is at rest. If an object is moving at a constant speed, it means it has the same increase in distance in a given time. Time is increasing to the right, and the distance is increasing constantly with time. The object moves at a constant speed. Constant speed is shown by straight lines on a graph. 419100 128905 Let’s look at two moving objects: Both of the lines on the graph show that each object moved the same distance, but the object shown by the steeper dashed line gets there before the other one. 476250 114935 In this case, a steeper line shows the same distance travelled but in a shorter time. Both lines are straight, so b o th speeds are constant. Graphs that show acceleration look different from those that show constant speed. 409575 155575 The line on this graph is curving upwards. This shows an increase in speed since the line is getting steeper. In a given time, the distance the object moves is getting larger, it is accelerating. uploads/science/mrsgren_setwork.pdf.searchText: MRS GREN Classification is a word used to describe the grouping of things according to their similarities. One of the most basic types of classification is to decide whether something is living or non-living. Living things are called organisms. The five things above can be readily separated into living and non-living. Living – fly, kiwi, cabbage. Non- living – fire, clouds. Here are the seven activities of all living things. If you remember that someone has an auntie called MRS GREN you will be able to remember all seven activities.  Movement  Reproduction  Respiration  Excretion  Sensitivity  Nutrition  Growth Most of this is common sense. You can move around from place to place and so can most animals. A few animals like barnacles can only do this when they are young larvae. Adult barnacles are firmly stuck onto the rock, but they can still move their legs to catch food. Animals move to: find shelter, escape from predators and other danger, find food, and find a mate. Respiration is the release of energy from glucose or another organic chemical in our cells. Respiration happens in ALL living things. Sensitivity is very important. How would you know if something was fit to eat if you could not smell or taste it? How would you escape danger? Plants sense water – their roots grow towards it. Growth. We all do it. Reproduction: Continuation of the species. Excretion means getting rid of the poisonous waste products from the chemical reactions in our bodies. We breathe out carbon dioxide and we urinate. Nutrition. We have to eat to provide the materials for growth, repair and to provide us with energy. Why was fire classified as non-living? To decide if something is living or non-living, run through each of the seven criteria of MRS GREN. If the answer is no to any of them, then the object is non-living. For fire: • Movement – yes • Respiration – no (uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, but obviously is not occurring in cells) • Sensitivity – yes/no (can respond to wind/water, etc) • Growth – yes • Reproduction – yes (a spark from one fire will cause another fire to start) • Excretion – yes (the smoke) • Nutrition – yes (the wood, paper, etc that it burns) As the answer was ‘no’ to respiration, fire is non-living, even though it carries out all the other activities. Respiration and breathing are not the same. Breathing is a mechanical process. When we breathe in, our diaphragm contracts and pulls down the base of our lungs, and intercostal muscles move the ribs out, stretching and enlarging the lungs, so that air is sucked in down our windpipe (via our nose or mouth). As we breathe out, our diaphragm and chest muscles relax, the lungs are no longer stretched and air is pushed back out of the lungs. Respiration involves the transfer of energy. The respiratory system is made up of the lungs and airways such as the windpipe, throat and nasal passages. Our lungs absorb oxygen from the air we breathe. The oxygen is transported around our body and used to ‘burn up’ the food we eat and convert it to energy. This results in the production of carbon dioxide, which is breathed out. Excretion is not getting rid of solid waste (faeces) but the elimination of the waste products of the chemical processes inside the cells (e.g. in urine, in exhaled air). Questions 1. What is another word that could be used to describe ‘classification’? 2. Split the following things up into living and non-living: a mushroom, a table, moss, butter, bacteria, ferns, distilled water, the wind, a cat. 3. Why were clouds classified as non-living? Run through each of the seven criteria of MRS GREN like the example for “fire” on the previous page. 4. The drawings show a wind-up toy dog, a rabbit and a rose bush. Use only the words in the list below to complete all the sentences. You may use the words more than once. eat grow move from place to place reproduce (i) In what way are the toy dog and the rabbit similar? Both the toy dog and the rabbit can (ii) Give two ways in which the toy dog is different from the rabbit. (a) The toy dog cannot…(b) The toy dog cannot…. (iii) Give two ways in which the rabbit is different from the rose bush. The rabbit can… 5. Copy and complete this table. Remember even plants move their leaves to get sunlight. APPLE TOY COMP- AERO- TIGER FOSSIL SNAKE TREE ROBOT UTER PLANE Does it  Move? Does it  Respire? Does it have  Sensitivity? Does it Grow? Does it Reproduce? Does it Excrete? Does it need Nutrition? SO IS IT Yes ALIVE? 6. In your own words, describe the difference between breathing and respiration.

One reason they are important is because, they help scientists understand the genetic patterns of diseases. It is important to be able to interpret pedigree charts in order to learn the pattern of a disease or condition. Specifically, using a pedigree chart, you can tell if the disease or condition is autosomal, X-linked, dominant, or recessive. Before you start this activity it is important to review several symbols: -Unaffected male - Affected male -Unaffected female -Affected female Procedure: A. First you need to become comfortable in making a pedigree chart. Complete the following examples. You may refer to your Pedigree PowerPoint notes if necessary. 1. How can you tell if a couple is married on a pedigree? Write a one-sentence description and draw an example. (1 point for description, 1 point for drawing) A circle and a square are connected by a line 2. How can you tell if the couple who is married had children? Write a one-sentence description and draw an example. (1 point for description, 1 point for drawing) The couple has a circle and square connected by a line. The children are connected by a line branching down from the married couple with the children symbols attached to that line. 3. Draw a pedigree that represents Mary married to Greg and with 2 sons (Scott and Tyler) and 1 daughter (Karen). Please label the pedigree with the names of the people. (3 points, each symbol must have labels) 4. Draw a pedigree that represents Mary married to Greg, with 2 sons (Scott and Tyler) and 1 daughter. Their son, Scott, married April and had Sutton (a boy) and Kendall (a girl). Their daughter, Karen, married Harry and had Eliq (a son) and Tariq (a son). Please label the pedigree with the names of the people. (3 points, each symbol must have labels) 5. Draw a pedigree that represents Julie married to Jeff, with one daughter, Josephine. Josephine married Joseph and had Jason and Joe. Joe married Julia and had Shannon and fraternal twin boys, Mark and Alex. Mark married Alison and had Ray and Scarlet. Please label the pedigree with the names of the people. (4 points, each symbol must have labels) A. Identify the following pedigree charts as autosomal, X-linked, recessive, and dominant. Please explain your answers. (3 points for each correct answer, including correct explanation) 1. Is the following autosomal or X-linked? Is it dominant or recessive? The following pedigree is X-linked. One reason is because most of the males in the pedigree have the disorder. This means that the mother is a carrier of the disorder and has given the gene to the sons on the X chromosome. The father cannot give the sons an X chromosome; he only gives them a Y chromosome. This pedigree is recessive due to the fact that neither parent has the disorder. This means the mother can be heterozygous and the father possesses a normal gene on the X chromosome. 2. Is the following autosomal or X-linked? Is it dominant or recessive? This pedigree is autosomal because both men and women equally have the disorder. This means the disorder is not found on the X chromosome, if it was found on the X chromosome, Most of the men would have the disorder and few women would have the disorder. The disorder is dominant, because a parent in each generation has the disorder. If it were recessive the parents would be heterozygous. 3. Is the following autosomal or X-linked? Is it dominant or recessive? This pedigree is autosomal because both men and women equally have the disorder. This means the disorder is not found on the X chromosome. If it were found on the X chromosome, most of the men would have the disorder and few women would have the disorder. This pedigree is recessive due to the fact that neither parent has the disorder. This means the mother is heterozygous and the father possesses a normal gene on the X chromosome. B. Now you must make a pedigree chart from the descriptions given. Tell whether it is autosomal or X-linked and whether it is dominant or recessive. Also, state which type of muscular dystrophy the pedigree could be based off of the list your teacher has given you. Label the pedigree with the names of the individuals. (2 points for correct chart including symbols with labels. 2 points for correct description and type of MD.) a. Chad and Veronica got married and had Brittany, Kristin, and Harry. It was discovered that Harry had muscular dystrophy. Brittany married Larry and had Stephan and Stephanie. Stephan also had muscular dystrophy. Larry’s brother Barry also had muscular dystrophy but neither of their parents had the disorder. Draw a pedigree: Is it Autosomal or X-linked? Is it Dominant or recessive? Name the types of muscular dystrophy this pedigree chart could represent. This is X-linked and recessive. It could be Duchenne or Emery-Dreifuss. These two forms of muscular dystrophy are X-linked and recessive. b. Lisa and Ashton got married and had three girls, Cari, Mary, and Terry. It was discovered that Lisa had muscular dystrophy. Terry married Perry and had two boys, Pike and Tike. It was discovered that Terry and Pike had muscular dystrophy. Draw a pedigree Is it autosomal or X-linked? Is it dominant or recessive? Name the types of muscular dystrophy this pedigree chart could represent. This is autosomal and dominant. This could be Distal, Emery-Dreifuss, or Limb-Girdle, because these forms of muscular dystrophy are autosomal and dominant c. Debbie married David and had three children, Darren, Dawn, and Derek. David, Darren and Derek discovered they have muscular dystrophy. Derek married Didi and had two children, Denise and Destiny. Denise also has muscular dystrophy and married Dirk. They had two children, Dee and Deven. Dee has muscular dystrophy. Draw a pedigree: Is it autosomal or X-linked? Is it dominant or recessive? This is autosomal and dominant. Name the types of muscular dystrophy this pedigree chart could represent. This pedigree is autosomal because both men and women equally have the disorder. The disorder is dominant, because a parent in each generation has the disorder. If it were recessive, the parents could be heterozygous. This could be distal, Erb’s fascioscapulohumeral, Grower’s, or limb-girdle, because these forms of muscular dystrophy are autosomal and dominant.

uploads/science/Naming Compounds and Wri.searchText: ﻿Naming Compounds & Writing Formula Metallic substances The name of the metallic substance is the same as the element. The formula is the element symbol. (sodium – Na, iron-Fe, copper-Cu etc) Ionic compounds Rules for naming: 1. The metal or positive ion is named first and keeps its normal name. 2. The non-metal or negative ion is named second and has the end of its name written as –ide, -ate or –ite. 3. If the metal ion has several valencies, indicate its valency using roman numerals. (sodium chloride, ammonium sulfate, iron sulfite etc) Writing formula: 1. The positive ion is written first. 2. The negative ion is written second. 3. The number of each ion is adjusted so that the total positive charge equals the total negative charge. Subscripts are used to indicate the number of each ion present. (sodium chloride-NaCl, ammonium phosphate- (NH4)3PO4, iron(II) hydroxide- Fe(OH)2) Covalent Compounds Rules for naming 1. The name of the element closer to the bottom left side of the periodic table is named first and keeps its normal name. 2. The name of the second element has its name changed to end in –ide e.g. sulphide, chloride, oxide, nitride etc 3. Prefixes are used to indicate the number of atoms of each element. 4. If there is only one atom of the first element then no prefix is used. For example, CO2 – carbon dioxide 5. Molecules composed of one element are given the name of that element. For example, H2-hydrogen, O2-oxygen, Cl2- chlorine Number of atoms Prefix Number of atoms Prefix 1 mono- 6 hexa- 2 di- 7 hepta- 3 tri- 8 octa- 4 tetra- 9 nona- 5 penta- 10 deca- Examples: 1. Zn - zinc 2. sodium iodide - NaI calcium nitrate – Ca(NO3)2 3. CuSO4 – copper(II) sulfate Fe2O3 – iron(iii) oxide 4. nitrogen trifluoride – NF3 Tetraphosphorus decaoxide – P4O10 Nitrogen gas – N2 5. SO3 – sulphur trioxide S2Cl4 –disulfur tetrachloride Exercises: 1. Name the following ionic compounds. a) ZnS b) Mg(OH)2 c) CuCO3 d) AlCl3 e) BaSO4 2. Write the correct formula for the following compounds. a) copper(II) chloride b) calcium hydroxide c) ammonium carbonate d) tin(II) sulfate e) chromium(III) phosphate f) silver chloride 3. Name the following covalent compounds. a) Br2 b) P2O5 c) SO2 d) HCl e) N2O4 4. Write the formula for the covalent compounds written below. a) oxygen dichloride b) carbon tetrafluoride c) hydrogen iodide d) silicon dioxide e) carbon monoxide

uploads/science/Naming_Compounds workshe.searchText: ﻿ Naming Compounds - (Chemical Formulae) Prefixes Mono _____________ Di _____________ Tri ___________ Tetra _____________ Pent _____________ Hex ___________ 7: _____________ 8: _____________ 9: ___________ 10: _____________ Naming covalent compounds of two non-metal elements 1. Covalent compounds are combinations of two or more non-metal elements. They are not ionic. 2. These compounds consist of molecules (eg, H2O, CO2, CO, SO3) in which atoms are sharing electrons so that each one has a full valence shell. 3. Some covalent compounds have “common names” that do not follow any particular set of rules. These must be learned - for example: Compound Common name Compound Common name H2O water CHCl3 chloroform CH4 methane HCl hydrogen chloride NH3 ammonia HBr hydrogen bromide H2O2 hydrogen peroxide HF hydrogen fluoride 4. For most other covalent compounds there are a number of rules to follow for naming them. 5. Naming rules (nomenclature) 1) The name of the first element in the formula is the same as the element itself. (eg; CO2 is carbon dioxide) 2) The name of the second element in the formula has its ending changed to IDE (eg; CO2 is carbon dioxide) 3) If there are more than one of the first element’s atoms, the prefixes di (2), tri (3), tetra (4), penta (5), hexa (6), hepta (7), octa (8), nona (9), deca (10) are used to show how many atoms there are. (eg; P4O10 is tetraphosphorus decoxide) 4) For the second element, the prefixes mono (1), di (2), tri (3), tetra (4), penta (5), hexa (6), hepta (7), octa (8), nona (9), deca (10) are used to show how many atoms there are. (eg; P4O10 is tetraphosphorus decoxide) Name these covalent compounds CO SO2 CO2 SO3 NO2 N2O3 N2O N2O5 Cl2O7 Br2O5 CH4 P2O3 P2O5 P4O6 NH3 SiF4 BF3 SF6 BrI5 OBr2 SiCl4 OF2 HCl H2O2 H2O SeCl2 NF3 PCl5 SiI4 IF7 B4O6 Write formulas for these covalent compounds Hydrogen sulfide Dinitrogen tetrachloride Sulfur pentabromide Selenium hexafluoride Nitrogen triiodide Tetraphosphorus hexasulfide Tetraphosphorus decasulfide Chlorine difluoride Oxygen dibromide Chlorine pentabromide Silicon tetrabromide Silicon tetrafluoride Disilicon hexachloride Disilicon hexabromide Methane Ammomia Sulfur tetrachloride Dinitrogen trisulfide Dibromine monoiodide Diselenium pentabromide Trisilicon octafluoride Tetrasilicon decachloride Diphosphorus tetrabromide Tellurium hexafluoride Tellurium trioxide Tellurium hexabromide Hexaphosphorus nonoxide Dicarbon trioxide Trisilicon diphosphide Boron monophosphide Astatine pentafluoride Naming Ionic compounds of one metal and one non-metal 1. Ionic compounds are formed between metals (left on the periodic table) and non-metals (right on the periodic table). 2. These compounds consist of a lattice of positive and negative ions. (eg, NaCl, AgNO3, Fe2O3) is which the metal has “donated” one or more eletrons to become positive, whilst the non-metal has accepted electrons to become negative. 3. Some ionic compounds have “common names” that do not follow any particular set of rules. These must be learned - for example: Compound Common name Compound Common name Fe2O3 rust NaCl Salt or table salt 4. For most other covalent compounds there are a number of rules to follow for naming them. 5. Naming rules (nomenclature) i) The Metal is named first and does not have its name changed, so it is written as seen in the periodic table. ii) The charge on the metal is indicated by roman numerals in brackets after its’ name. This is not necessary for metals that only exist in one state. (eg. Sodium is written as Na, because it only comes as Na+, whilst iron would have to be written as Fe(II) or Fe(III), as it exists as Fe2+ and Fe3+. iii) The non-metal ion has a suffix added which indicates its’ charge or form. Suffixes may be –ide, -ite, -ate, depending on the number of oxygen atoms that are included with the element. per- -ate greatest number of oxygen atoms -ate greater -ite smaller hypo- -ite smallest number of oxygen atoms iv) At this stage you will be using the list of ions, periodic tables and all notes in order to determine the names and formula/symbols for the ion. uploads/science/Natural Ecosystems Notes.searchText: Natural Ecosystems (p 281 -285 ) Organisms live surrounded by other organisms and by non-living things such as rocks, water and soil. What is a habitat ? How is a habitat different from an environment? Ecosystems What is an ecosystem ? What are the three main components of ecosystems ? Factors Influencing Organisms Organisms in an ecosystem can be affected by two main sets of factors: the actions of living organisms and the non-living surroundings. What are abiotic factors ? Give two examples. What are biotic factors ? Give two examples. Complete the table below to show some abiotic factors in an ecosystem by explaining how each factor can affect living organisms. Abiotic factor (physical factor) How this factor can affect living organisms Water Temperature Fire Light Soil minerals Gas level Complete the table below by giving the definition and an example of each of the biotic factors in an ecosystem. uploads/science/Natural Selection V2.doc.searchText: ﻿Natural Selection Experiment Aim: To simulate the process of natural selection Materials: 3 pieces of card, 1 white (snow), 1 brown (desert), 1 green (grassland) 1 set of 60 animals (30 brown and 30 white) Blu-tac Stopwatch Method 1. Select a habitat. 2. Choose one person to be the hunter and one person to be the time keeper and recorder. 3. The hunter closes their eyes while the timekeeper spreads the animals out on the habitat. 4. Once the animals are laid out, the hunter will have 20 seconds to ‘eat’ as many animals as they can by picking them up with the Blu-tac and putting them in a small pile. 5. Count the number of animals of each type eaten and record it in the table below 6. Repeat the experiment twice more with the same habitat and calculate an average. 7. Change to a different habitat and repeat the process. Results Desert Habitat Trial 1 Trial 2 Trial 3 Average No. of brown animals at start No. of brown animals eaten No. of white animals at start No. of white animals eaten Snow Habitat Trial 1 Trial 2 Trial 3 Average No. of brown animals at start No. of brown animals eaten No. of white animals at start No. of white animals eaten Grassland Habitat Trial 1 Trial 2 Trial 3 Average No. of brown animals at start No. of brown animals eaten No. of white animals at start No. of white animals eaten Conclusions and Questions What do you notice about how many animals are eaten and the colour of the background habitat? How can this be related to real animals and the adaptations they have? If your animals were real animals in the wild, they would reproduce. Assuming each animal produces offspring with the same adaptations, in this case colour, what do you think would happen to the population over successive generations in each habitat? In your own words, describe the process of natural selection.

uploads/science/Navigational Vectors.doc.searchText: Navigational Vectors Distance 1. Imagine you live in a regional town in WA and you need to plot a flight path to fly your private plane to Perth. Locate your home town on the map of WA, and draw a line between your home town and Perth airport. 2. This line represents the distance between the two towns and is a scalar value. Use the scale on the map to calculate the actual distance in km. Length of line on map: ________________ Distance in km: ___________ Can you plot a flight path from your home to Perth if you know distance alone? Of course not, direction is also an important factor. 3. Using a compass rose on your map find the direction that a pilot would need to head the plane to go from your hometown to your state capital. Express your direction as a degree heading from North (0º). _________________ 4. Now express the distance and direction together (example: 10 km at 37 o ). Distance and d irection, together, is called displacement . Displacement is a vector . __________________ 5. Now check your answer online. __________________ Scalars and Vectors A scalar is just a regular number. You've been using scalars for a long time now. Your height, how many dollars you have, and how much time has gone by in this class so far -all of these are scalars. No big deal, right? The only information a scalar gets across is the size of something, which we call magnitude. Scalars only have a magnitude, or size. A vector is like an "enhanced" number. It also has a magnitude (size), but in addition, it contains a direction, which is usually given in degrees. Because of this, a vector is written differently than a scalar. The most common way of writing a vector is to draw it using an arrow. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, and the direction the arrow is pointing in represents...well, the direction. Here's an example: 1930400 98425 If you took out a ruler and measured the length of the arrow that would be the vector's magnitude. And the direction is due East . (If we set North as 0º, which is what pilots do, then the vector above has a direction of 90º.) So, now do you see why distance is a scalar and displacement is a vector? Distance is simply how far you have moved, while displacement is where you are in relation to where you started out from. Draw a vector on your map from your hometown to your state capital. Is the tail or the head of the vector at the state capital? ___________________________ The following information is important for pilots to know for any airplane flight. Which of these quantities are vectors and which are scalars? Why? Number of passengers Plane speed Plane velocity Distance travelled Flight displacement Flight duration Plane Altitude Acceleration of plane Deceleration of plane Amount of fuel needed Give examples of other vector and scalar quantities that you use or encounter every day. In what other areas other than flight would knowledge of vectors be useful? Imagine that you are a pilot ready to fly between two cities. You must first file a flight plan. What do you think should go in a flight plan? Choose any two cities, devise your own version of a flight plan for this trip, and share it with the rest of the class. Graphical Addition of Vectors Your Mission: Plan a flight from your state capital to Sydney, NSW with a stopover in Coober Pedy. Locate a map of the Australia and find your state capital on the map. Draw a vector from your state capital to Coober Pedy. Using a ruler, compass rose or protractor, and the map, determine the flight's: Distance (km) Directional heading in degrees (as measured from 0º North) Displacement Draw another vector from Coober Pedy to Sydney. Again using a ruler, compass rose or protractor, and the map, determine this flight's: Distance (km) Directional heading in degrees (as measured from 0º North) Displacement Check your displacements for each leg of the flight online. Displacement from state capital to Coober Pedy (km and degrees) Displacement from Coober Pedy to Sydney (km and degrees) B) How far has the plane travelled? 1. Find the total distance the plane travelled by adding the distance that each vector represents. 2. Does this value indicate how far the final destination is from the origin? How far is the plane from your state capital at the end of the trip? The value that you are looking for is the total displacement which is the distance and direction from the point of origin to your final destination. To determine this you must add the vectors: Vector Addition Instructions Draw the first vector on your map (your state capital to Coober Pedy). Draw the second vector on your map (Coober Pedy to Sydney) with the tail of this vector beginning at the head of the first vector. Draw a third vector called the resultant from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second v ector. Measure the length of the resultant vector (km) and its directional heading (degrees) from your state capital. This resultant represents the total displacement of the plane. What is the resultant displacement of the plane from your state capital to S ydney (as m easured from your vector diagram)? How did your measured displacement compare with the displacement found using the i nternet? Think of a situation (other than flying) where it would be preferable to know displacement rather than distance travelled. Think of a situation (other than flying) where it would be preferable to know distance t ravelled rather than displacement. Create a vector game or puzzle for your classmates to solve. It could be a board game, a maze, a riddle, a mystery, a treasure hunt or anything else that you wish. It should use 5 vectors. Trade games/puzzles with your classmates and see if they solve it correctly. Wind Velocity Flying in the w ind Imagine that you are walking in a cyclone with howling winds a ll around you. How will the w ind affect your movement if it is blowing: at your back directly towards you from the side Flying a plane in the wind can produce the same effect. A pilot generally wants to fly in the shortest path between two cities. Why? Well, it saves time and fuel. The wind, however, may prevent her from doing this. How can the wind affect a plane's flight? What does a pilot need to do to compensate for the wind? B) Determining Wind Velocity Winds in the northern hemisphere normally blow from west to east. This can change dramatically, however, when there is a front moving across the continent. Velocity is another example of a vector. Wind velocity is indicated by the wind speed and direction. Pilots use wind maps that show the wind velocity at the altitude of the plane. A special symbol on the map called a wind barb shows the both the speed and direction of the wind (wind velocity). C) Resultant Velocity Imagine that you are flying a plane over your home state. Your altitude is 14 ,000 feet. The controls in the plane are set so that you are headed due North at 400km/h. Draw a vector to represent your plane's velocity. Make sure to draw it to scale. What was the wind velocity (speed in km/h and direction) over your home state at 14 ,000 f eet? Draw this wind velocity vector so that its tail is at the head of your plane's velocity vector. Make sure to draw it to scale. What is the plane's resultant velocity? Create a special notation or symbol to describe a river current of 4 m/s flowing south-east and explain how to read it. Find examples of how wind affects sports activities, architectural designs, or other real world applications. D ) A captain is heading his boat directly across a river with a very strong current. As the first mate, you must advise him how the river current will affect the boat's movement. Prepare a drawing that you can use to show the captain the boat's resultant velocity. Make up a football, soccer, or other sports play that uses two or more vectors at right angles to each other. Write out the details of the play as if you were an announcer covering the game. Then give the sports play to one of your classmates and have your classmate find the displacement of the play using the Pythagorean Theorem and one of the trig functions.
